title: microprofiler-snapshots-python-tokenize-parse-threadpool-notes
body:
Purpose:
Capture and interpret microprofiler snapshots targeting CPU-side bottlenecks observed in recent production traces (Nov 2025 — Feb 2026). Focus areas: tokenization work per request, request-parsing overhead (header/body), Python threadpool utilization and GIL/GC interactions.

Context / motivation:
- Several customer incidents reported tail latency spikes (p95/p99) for short-chat requests (avg tokens <= 64).
- Initial flamegraphs from canary pools pointed to a large share of CPU time in pure-Python tokenizers and request-parsing code paths, plus GC pauses for some request patterns.
- We need an actionable mitigation plan: incremental changes that reduce CPU per-request cost and latency tail without large infra changes.

What we measured (summary):
- Workload: 10k requests over 10 minutes from synthetic client (concurrent=200, seq_len <= 64).
- Baseline p50/p95/p99: 18ms / 92ms / 270ms for small text completions on dedicated GPU + frontend host.
- CPU attribution (py-spy sampling, aggregated):
  - Python tokenizer functions (tokenizer.encode/normalize): ~32% of sampled CPU
  - request_parsing.py::parse_http_body + header parsing: ~18%
  - threadpool worker scheduling (concurrent.futures) + queue ops: ~9%
  - GC (collect/pause): ~6% (spikes correlated with long-lived request bursts)
  - runtime bookkeeping (metrics, tracing serialization): ~7%
  - other native extensions (ssl, socket read): remainder

Key flamegraph observations (raw notes):
- Tokenizer hotspots concentrated in calls to byte->unicode normalization, regex splitting, and per-token detokenization helper loops. Many calls reallocate small strings.
- parse_http_body does a two-pass decode: read bytes -> .decode('utf-8', 'replace') -> json.loads, with some validation loops over keys. This is heavy for small payloads.
- ThreadPoolExecutor.submit overhead visible on p95: workers do tiny tasks (tokenize + small preprocessing) but scheduling dominates when tasks are sub-ms.
- Periodic GC collections coincide with micro-bursts; objects allocated by tokenizer are short-lived but many. Increasing allocation rate triggers more frequent incremental collections.

Commands / tooling used (for reproducibility):
- py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python -m my_client.load_test --c=200 --t=600
- perf record -F 99 -g --pid <frontend-pid> -o perf.data
- perf script | ./FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > flame.svg
- python -m cProfile -o cprof.out serving/frontend/request_parsing.py
- tracemalloc snapshots before/after stress test to confirm allocation sites

Representative profiler extracts (annotated):
- tokenizer.py:normalize_text  28.6%  (heavy unicode ops)
- tokenizer.py:byte_to_str  12.4%  (calls allocate small bytes objects)
- request_parsing.py:parse_json_body  17.6%  (json.loads dominates)
- request_router.py:handle_incoming  5.2%  (scheduling + tracing)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) The pure-Python tokenizer implementation is the largest single contributor to CPU and p99 for small requests. Replacing hot paths with a C-accelerated tokenizer would give immediate wins.
2) Request parsing does redundant work for small JSON payloads; a fast-path that handles compact inference request shapes (no validation, direct buffer decode) would reduce overhead.
3) Threadpool per-task overhead hurts when tasks are extremely small: batching tasks inside worker threads or moving to long-lived workers avoids scheduling costs.
4) GC pauses are reactive; reducing allocations (via buffers or reuse) and tuning thresholds reduces occasional tail spikes.

Short-term mitigations (low-risk, quick):
- Add a "fast-path" in request_parsing: if content-length < 1KB and body looks like simple inference request, use orjson.loads(b) and skip key validation. (Benchmark: expected ~2-3x faster parse).
- Switch tokenizer to use a cached bytes->str buffer and avoid creating intermediate lists for ascii-only inputs. Feature-flag under EXPERIMENT_TOKENIZER_FASTPATH.
- Increase worker task granularity: change frontend to submit combined (tokenize + preprocess) as single task to threadpool instead of separate steps. Measure p95 improvement.
- GC tuning: set PYTHONMALLOC=malloc? (experiment) and bump gc thresholds for ephemeral services to reduce frequency during bursts.

Medium-term mitigations (medium-risk):
- Introduce a small C-extension for the hot tokenizer functions (normalize_text, byte_to_str) using the same public tokenizer API. Pro: minimal infra change; Con: C-extension maintenance + cross-platform builds.
- Replace ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded async worker pool (uvloop + bg tasks) to reduce scheduling overhead for many tiny synchronous tasks.

Longer-term (higher effort):
- Move tokenization into the serving runtime binary (C++/Rust) and expose a lightweight RPC from frontend to runtime on localhost; this centralizes tokenization and avoids repeated allocations.
- Rework request parsing to a streaming parser that operates on bytes without intermediate Python objects for common request shapes.

Experiment plan (concrete steps, owners, metrics):
1) Fast-path parse: Diego to implement orjson fast-path, measure parse latency and CPU; success: parse CPU < 25% of previous per-request parse cost; rollout flag: parse-fastpath. (2 days dev + 1 day canary)
2) Task coalescing: Marina to change task boundaries, run load test at c=400 to measure p95; success: p95 decreases by >=15% on frontend host. (1 day)
3) Tokenizer micro-optimizations: Aisha to add buffer reuse and remove regex in common ascii branch; measure delta. If wins <10%, escalate to C-extension exploration. (3 days)
4) GC thresholds: SRE to run controlled experiments with env overrides during flash loads; measure GC time and p99 spikes. (1 day)

Measurement checklist for each experiment:
- Controlled load: synthetic client reproducer (same seed), at least 10k requests, concurrent 200/400 depending on test.
- Collect: py-spy sampling profile, perf, tracemalloc delta, GC stats, a 1-minute flamegraph from steady-state window
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (request-level), CPU per request, frontend host CPU utilization, allocation rate (bytes/sec)

Open questions / risks:
- C-extension build complexity for our distribution (many customers run private). Need cross-compile story.
- Are we optimizing the right place? Some apps offload tokenization entirely client-side — need customer telemetry to see who would benefit.
- Orjson vs json: correctness for all edge cases? We must add tests for byte-order marks and invalid UTF-8 payloads.

Next steps (short):
- Kick off fast-path parse PR (INF-4823) and link smoke results in the PR description.
- Run experiment 2 (task coalescing) in canary pool this week.
- If fast-path + coalescing together give >=20% p95 improvement, schedule tokenizer C-extension spike.

Notes-to-self / random fragments: 
- consider pybind11 for tokenizer C-ext prototype, keep API mirrors for python tests
- check for hidden cost of tracing (OpenTelemetry): spinner shows serialization cost ~3.5% — maybe postpone heavy traces on fast-path requests
- capture a small reproducible test case for unit tests (random ascii vs emoji heavy)

References / links used while profiling:
- Flamegraph outputs: s3://redwood-profiles/serving-runtime/2026-02-12/fronted-flame.svg
- py-spy runs attached to PR 874
- Perf notes: /mnt/profiles/perf-2026-02-18.txt

TODOS:
- [ ] Add smoke script to PR to run quick py-spy snapshot
- [ ] Add orjson safe tests
- [ ] Collect customer telem on tokenization (who passes raw text vs pre-tokenized)

Decision log (for reviewers):
- If orjson fast-path passes tests and reduces parse CPU by >=30%, we will enable by default for hosted API 2.0 and put opt-out env for private installs.
- Tokenizer C-ext will be attempted only after micro-optimizations plateau (>=1 sprint of low benefit).

-- Marina
(working notes; will convert to a cleaned-up RFC if experiments validate wins)
